metaDescription: Six cordless leaf blowers at or under $150, compared on pack size, brand platforms and real airflow for mid-sized yards and heavier autumn cleanup.
expertTake: The EWZ with its single large pack is the pick for runtime on a bigger lot, and the WORX WG547 is the safe value choice because it sits on an established 20V battery platform. Anyone with an acre of trees or who wants gas-class clearing should look past this class entirely.
introParagraphs: At this level the story shifts from basic kits to battery strategy. Some makers put a very large pack in the box, while established brands sell a smaller pack that fits a wider family of tools.
That choice, one big pack versus a platform you can reuse, matters more than the headline airflow figure. Prices move, and the $150 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: EWZ 750 CFM Cordless Blower 10.0Ah Battery
products.description:
The EWZ stands out for its 10.0Ah battery, which stores far more energy than the 2.0Ah to 6.0Ah packs elsewhere in this list. Energy in the pack is what turns a short burst of turbo into a real working session, and the listing claims long runtime at lower speeds. The headline 750 CFM and 250 MPH are maker figures, and the turbo mode that reaches them will drain even a large pack quickly.

The tradeoff is weight and a single pack. A 10Ah cell stack is heavy to hold out in front of you, and with one battery you cannot swap mid job. Compared with the PTBGLV, which pairs two 6.0Ah packs, you gain more capacity per pack but lose the ability to keep working while one charges.

Check the charger time, since a large pack on a slow charger can take hours to refill. Store the pack partly charged and away from freezing. It is for owners with a mid-sized lot who prefer one long session over swapping. Budget a few minutes at the end of a session to let the pack cool before charging it, since a hot large cell charges less efficiently and ages faster than one that has rested.
products.bestFor: Longer single sessions on a mid-sized yard.
pros: Large 10.0Ah pack stores the most energy here
Highest airflow and speed claims in the group
cons: Single pack means no mid-job swap
Heavy pack adds fatigue over a long session

products.name: WORX WG547 20V Cordless Blower 360 CFM
products.description:
The WG547 uses a turbine fan to push a claimed 360 CFM, a more modest figure than the EWZ but backed by an established brand. Its big advantage is the battery: it belongs to a 20V family that WORX sells across other yard tools, so the pack can serve more than one machine.

The two speed modes are basic, and the claim does not match the 700-plus CFM figures on lesser-known listings. In practice, a name-brand 360 CFM often moves air comparably to an inflated 650 CFM claim from an obscure brand, because the measurement methods differ.

Parts and replacement packs are easier to find for a mainstream platform, which matters in year three when the original pack fades. Store the battery indoors. It suits a buyer who wants a dependable blower and may add other tools on the same pack. If you already own a battery tool from a big brand, compare the cost of this kit against simply buying a bare WORX-style tool, because the second charger and pack may duplicate gear you have.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want an established battery platform.
pros: Battery platform can power other tools
Turbine fan design is efficient for its size
cons: Lower airflow claim than the EWZ

products.name: PTBGLV 21V Cordless Blower 2 x 6.0Ah 6-Speed
products.description:
This kit ships with two 6.0Ah packs, which is 12 amp hours in total, close to the EWZ's single 10.0Ah pack but with the swap advantage. While one pack charges, the other works, so you can clear a large lawn without waiting.

Six speed levels give finer control than the WORX, and the 21V label is simply the maker's peak voltage for what is a typical 18V nominal pack. The output is bounded by that voltage class regardless of how much energy the packs hold.

Expect the usual import caveats on support and parts. Rotate packs and store them cool. It is a good fit if you value the two-pack workflow and variable control over brand name. Because the voltage class is the limit, treat the 12Ah total as endurance rather than extra force; the blower will not push harder, it will simply keep pushing for more minutes.
pros: Two 6.0Ah packs allow continuous work with swapping

products.name: YOOVL 650 CFM Cordless Blower 2 x 5.2Ah
products.description:
The YOOVL balances pack size and control, with two 5.2Ah packs and three speed settings. Its total stored energy sits between the PTBGLV and the entry kits, and the 650 CFM claim is moderate for this class.

Three speed levels cover most jobs without the complexity of a six-step dial. Compared with the PTBGLV, you give up a little capacity and finer control, but gain a design that is easier to understand.

Maintain it like any lithium tool: rotate packs, keep the intake clean and store at partial charge. It is for the buyer who wants a sensible middle kit without chasing extremes. It is a sensible middle choice for an owner who wants two packs but does not want to chase the biggest airflow number on the page.
products.bestFor: Mid-sized lawns wanting a balanced kit.
pros: Two 5.2Ah packs for solid run time
Moderate claims are easier to trust
cons: Less airflow claim than the EWZ

products.name: ALSO GO Cordless Blower 600 CFM 150 MPH 2 x 4.0Ah
products.description:
The ALSO GO pairs a 600 CFM claim with a lower 150 MPH speed, a volume-focused profile that suits moving piles of dry leaves. Two 4.0Ah packs give moderate run time, and two speed modes keep it simple.

The lower air speed means it is weaker at peeling damp leaves off pavement than the EWZ. It is a straightforward choice if your debris is mostly dry and loose.

Store packs partly charged and keep the intake clear. It is a good middle-of-the-road choice between the WORX and the larger-pack kits. Pair it with a rake for the thick, matted corners of a yard, because a volume blower works best on the loose top layer rather than packed leaf mats.
products.bestFor: Dry leaf piles on open lawns.
pros: Volume-focused airflow suits dry leaf piles
Two packs and a charger included
cons: Lower air speed claim than rivals

products.name: Greenworks 40V Cordless Blower 135 CFM 2.0Ah
products.description:
Greenworks lists the lowest airflow here at 135 CFM, but it comes in a 40V family that shares batteries with a wide range of mowers, trimmers and saws. For an owner investing in a single battery system, the pack matters more than the blower.

The 2.0Ah pack is small, so run time is short. This is a sweeper for porches and driveways, not a leaf-pile mover.

If you already own Greenworks 40V tools, a bare-tool purchase makes more sense. It is for buyers who value platform over performance. Think of it as a porch and driveway tool that happens to share a battery with larger machines, and the purchase makes much more sense than judging its airflow alone.
products.bestFor: Owners building around a 40V battery family.
pros: Proven brand with replacement parts available
cons: Lowest airflow claim of the group

buyingCriteria.criterion: One big pack versus two packs
buyingCriteria.explanation: The EWZ ships one 10.0Ah pack while the PTBGLV ships two 6.0Ah packs, totalling 12Ah. One large pack runs longer in a single go, but two packs let you charge one while using the other. For a large lawn, the swap workflow usually beats a single heavy pack. Heavy packs also change balance, so hold a demo unit or read owner comments about fatigue before committing to the biggest cell.

The WORX 20V and Greenworks 40V packs belong to families you can reuse for other tools. A no-name pack serves one device. If you plan to add a trimmer or mower, platform value outweighs a slightly bigger airflow claim. Reusing a pack across tools also lowers the number of chargers on your garage shelf and the number of different batteries you must keep alive each winter.

The EWZ at 750 CFM, YOOVL at 650 and WORX at 360 span a wide range partly due to measurement method. Compare packs and motor class before airflow. A 21V or 20V pack cannot sustain gas-class output. Ask whether the number is measured at the nozzle with a concentrator fitted, since that inflates speed while shrinking volume.

The ALSO GO leans on 600 CFM with 150 MPH for pile moving, while the EWZ claims 250 MPH for loosening debris. Match to your yard: open lawn favors volume, pavement and wet leaves favor speed. If your lawn is open and flat, volume wins; if leaves collect against fences and in beds, speed and a narrow nozzle matter more.

Six levels on the PTBGLV give control, and a turbo mode on the EWZ gives a short boost. Turbo drains packs quickly, so use it sparingly. A boost button is useful for a minute at a time, not for the whole job, and it also makes the motor louder.

A 10Ah pack on the EWZ adds heft to the handle. Lighter kits like the ALSO GO are easier on the wrist. If you clean for long periods, weigh the pack as much as the claim. A comfortable grip and a balanced tube reduce the real fatigue that cuts sessions short far more than a weak claim does.

specDecoder.meaning: Amp hours of one pack, and the sum across the kit. Total tells you work capacity.
specDecoder.watchFor: The PTBGLV has 12Ah across two packs, the EWZ has 10Ah in one.

specDecoder.meaning: The battery family, such as 20V or 40V. Same family packs interchange.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Greenworks 40V pack will not fit a WORX 20V tool.

specDecoder.meaning: Air volume claim. More volume moves piles faster.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EWZ claims 750 CFM and the Greenworks 135 CFM, but methods differ.

specDecoder.meaning: Air speed claim for loosening stuck debris.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EWZ claims 250 MPH versus the ALSO GO at 150, which changes wet-leaf performance.

specDecoder.meaning: A short high-output boost on top of normal settings.
specDecoder.watchFor: It can empty a pack in minutes, so do not plan runtime around it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery energy
howWeEvaluated.description: We summed amp hours across each kit and checked pack count. The PTBGLV at 12Ah total and EWZ at 10Ah led. Small single packs lost points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform value
howWeEvaluated.description: We credited packs that fit a broader tool family, such as WORX 20V and Greenworks 40V. Proprietary one-off packs scored lower for long-term value.

howWeEvaluated.title: Claim plausibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared airflow claims to the voltage class and motor behind them. A 750 CFM claim from a 21V-class tool was treated cautiously.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted speed steps and boost modes. Six levels on the PTBGLV scored best.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at parts support, charger inclusion and brand history. Owner feedback patterns informed the durability view.

cards.label: Big pack
cards.text: The EWZ and PTBGLV maximize stored energy, giving long sessions, but the packs serve only that tool.

cards.label: Platform
cards.text: The WORX and Greenworks packs power other tools, spreading cost, but ship with smaller capacity.

howToChoose.note: Choose a big pack if the blower is your only battery tool; choose a platform if more tools will follow.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Large stored energy and a speed high enough to move matted leaves. Wet leaves weigh far more, so work in passes.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The EWZ with a 10.0Ah pack and 250 MPH claim is the best fit, and the PTBGLV is the choice if you prefer swapping.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want a brushless 40V or higher platform that powers a mower too. Output beyond this band comes from voltage, not just bigger packs.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You have a small lot. The ALSO GO or WORX covers it comfortably.

maintenance.task: Charge both packs before big jobs
maintenance.why: Full packs let you swap without waiting. Check the charger lights.
Debris starves the fan and raises temperature.
Lithium cells age faster when stored full or empty. Keep them indoors.
A loose nozzle leaks air. Re-seat it until it clicks.
Grass dust blocks cooling slots and heats the motor.

faq.q: Is a 10.0Ah pack better than two smaller packs?
faq.a: It runs longer in one go but cannot be swapped. Two 6.0Ah packs let you charge one while using the other, which suits long jobs.
Treat them as best-case maker figures. A battery blower cannot sustain gas-class output, so use claims to rank within a brand.

faq.q: Should I buy into a battery platform?
faq.a: If you may add a trimmer or mower, yes. A platform pack serves several tools and spreads the cost.
Only for short bursts on stubborn debris. It drains the pack quickly and raises motor temperature.

faq.q: How long will the batteries last?
faq.a: Expect fade after several seasons. Store them cool and partly charged to slow it.
Prices move, and the $150 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated. Check the current figure before you buy.
